quote: You should meditate upon this thought until you attain enlightenment as to how the rest of the planet thinks about probability.
content: The subjects were not buying a separate good. They said that they "felt they had a better chance" with more red beans, which is a false feeling about probability, the thing the essay is describing. Low stakes do not make that feeling correct. They make it cheap to act on, which is why the experiment could expose it. Peters and colleagues found the ratio bias concentrated among the less numerate, which gives "the rest of the planet" its size (Peters et al. 2006). In international adult skills surveys, roughly a quarter to a third of adults in rich countries score at or below the lowest numeracy level. The essay's sarcastic "meditate until you attain enlightenment" addresses the numerate reader who assumes everyone else thinks in ratios, and Peters confirms that most people do not.

quote: According to ordinary economic theory, return and risk should correlate positively
content: The low-volatility anomaly cannot explain Ganzach's pattern because of the familiarity split. The same analysts, judging stocks in the same market, gave risk and return judgments that correlated positively for familiar stocks and negatively for unfamiliar ones (Ganzach 2000). If they were tracking a real cross-sectional anomaly, it would show up in the stocks they knew best. It showed up only where they knew least, and Ganzach found both judgments predicted by a single global evaluation of the stock. That is the affect heuristic. Behavioural finance has also proposed the affect-driven judgment itself as one explanation of the anomaly: lottery-like, exciting stocks attract optimistic buyers and are overpriced. The anomaly, if anything, is what the affect heuristic looks like in market prices.

quote: Yamagishi showed that subjects judged a disease as more dangerous when it was described as killing 1,286 people out of every 10,000, versus a disease that was 24.14% likely to be fatal.
content: "Present the same person with both and they choose correctly" is refuted a few paragraphs later in the same essay. Denes-Raj and Epstein put 7-in-100 and 1-in-10 side by side, in joint evaluation, and many subjects still chose the worse bowl, knowing it was worse (Denes-Raj & Epstein 1994). Denominator neglect survives having the comparison in view. Fable's own label for the effect, "denominator neglect," names a bias that persists in within-subject designs, and it is why Reyna and Brainerd recommend a fixed denominator even for readers who will see both numbers. The effect is one of format, as Fable says, and the essay's point is that formats reach judgment through affect, with or without the comparison.
